newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Cyclone ravages Bangladesh, kills five.
newsitem.headline: Cyclone ravages Bangladesh, kills five.

text.p: Five people were killed and at least 100 injured as a severe cyclone smashed into the Bangladesh coast and port city of Chittagong on Monday, officials said.
Doctors at Chittagong Medical College Hospital said they feared the death toll would rise as more reports came in.
"This was a major devastation and we think many more casualties will follow," one doctor said.
Officials in Chittagong said thousands of houses were demolished and uprooted trees and power poles jammed roads. Power supplies and communications were cut in many areas.
"We fear more severe damage in Cox's Bazar and Teknaf areas along the southeastern coast," one Chittagong official said.
Two opposition legislators said more than 100,000 houses were damaged on the outskirts of Chittagong city alone.
Port officials said one ship broke anchor, another vessel was damaged and a large crane crashed on a jetty during the 200 kph (124 mph) storm.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina cancelled a trip abroad and said she hoped Bangladeshis would face the crisis with courage. She assured them there would be no dearth of relief materials.
More than 100 medical teams were on standby to help victims.
The storm roared in from the Bay of Bengal and lashed the Bangladesh coast on Monday afternoon, sweeping Cox's Bazar and Teknaf areas, officials said.

"Vast areas have been affected, with electricity supply and telecommunications disrupted. Many houses have been destroyed and we can see sheets of tin from roof tops flying like tree leaves," Cox's Bazar district administrator Ali Imam Majumder told Reuters.

Weather officials said they feared the cyclone could trigger a tidal surge of up to five metres (15 ft), inundating widespread areas. They said Chittagong port city was also battered by winds of more than 200 kph (124 mph) and rain.
Communications have been cut with Teknaf and Cox's Bazar and Red Crescent officials said Teknaf may have suffered major damage.

Saint Martin's island near Teknaf was under two metres (six ft) of water. Several other islands had been battered by the cyclone and could be inundated, Red Crescent said quoting their field volunteers.
The full estimate of damage would not be available until Tuesday, disaster management officials said.
Bangladesh's worst cyclone in 1991 killed at least 138,000 people and left millions homeless.

"Damage from the latest cyclone could be more than in 1991," said Sajedur Rahman, director of Dhaka's Meterology office. "Casualties are expected to be much lower (than 1991) because we got enough time to warn, alert and evacuate people."
Information ministry officials said one million people had been evacuated from the cyclone's path by more than 33,000 Red Crescent and other volunteers.
Authorities fear high seas will flood large low-lying areas in the disaster-prone South Asian country. Rice crops and shrimp beds are likely to be affected, agriculture officials said.
"There are no significant crops, except for some rice, in the fields now but shrimp cultivation may be badly affected," said M.A. Wadud, chairman of Bangladesh Agriculture Development Corporation.

Fishermen have been warned not to leave port and coastal officials told to hoist "great danger" signals. Dozens of ships berthed at Chittagong and Mongla ports were moved to outer anchorages, port officials said.
"We are taking this precaution so the ships do not collide during the storm and jam the channel by sinking," said Chittagong Port Harbourmaster Quamrul Islam.
As state-run radio and television broadcast frequent storm warnings, hundreds of women held open-air prayers in Dhaka seeking divine protection against the impending disaster.
People fleeing their homes or being moved to cyclone shelters were asked to store drinking water, food and other essentials underground to help them after the cyclone.
